definition: Officious means offering unwanted advice or services.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word officious. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know officious should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: An officious passenger stood at the carousel directing everyone's luggage onto 'the correct side of the belt.'
Attentive stops short of officious — the attentive waiter notices what you need, while the officious one decides it for you.
Overbearing goes further than officious — the officious meddler pushes unwanted help, while the overbearing one takes charge of your affairs outright.

Meddlesome means poking into other people's private affairs — reading the mail, prying into the argument, asking questions that are none of your business. Officious intrusion is bossier: it hands out instructions and 'help' nobody requested. The meddlesome want to know your business; the officious want to run it.

Interfering means getting in the way of what others are doing — blocking or disrupting it, whether or not any 'help' is offered. Officious is a particular style of interfering: interference dressed up as assistance, from someone acting as if they had authority. All officious people interfere; not every interferer is officious.

Officious means offering unwanted advice or services.

The new hire meant well but arrived officious: by Friday he had reorganized a supply closet nobody had asked about, taped laminated instructions above the coffee maker, and 'corrected' three colleagues' voicemail greetings.
Officious is not 'official': an official acts with real authority, while an officious person supplies direction nobody requested—help so insistent that it becomes interference.
Officious is the precise word for uninvited supervision — the self-appointed expert straightening everyone else's work.
Do not let its look fool you: official means having real authority, officious means acting as if you did.
Its unit-mate punctilious is fussy about their own conduct; the officious are fussy about yours.

When Dara joined the community garden, she expected weeding, not supervision.
A longtime member named Hal appointed himself her guide.
He repositioned her tomato stakes while she was still setting them, rewrote the label on her plot, and left a laminated watering schedule on her bench.
Dara had not asked for any of this.

Other gardeners rolled their eyes in sympathy; Hal held no office in the club, but his officious coaching arrived daily, delivered with the certainty of a man who believed the garden could not survive without him.
When Dara finally thanked him and said she preferred to learn by her own mistakes, Hal looked wounded — he had never once considered that his help was not wanted.
